unit.title: Manage self as a board member

summary: This unit teaches you to manage yourself as a member of the board of a Jamaican public body. You will learn what the board is for and how it differs from management, the legal and ethical duties you owe, how to prepare for and contribute at meetings, how to handle conflicts of interest, gifts, confidentiality and the media, how to manage your time and workload, how to raise concerns, and how to review and develop your own performance.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to serve well as a **board member** of a public body, such as a statutory body, an executive agency, a school board, a regional health authority or a development agency. The unit is about **you**: your duties, your behaviour, your preparation, your time and your development.

A **board** is the group of people appointed to govern an organisation. It does not run the daily work: it sets direction, oversees performance, risk and money, appoints and holds the chief executive officer (CEO) to account, and answers for the body to the Minister, Parliament and the public. As a board member you act as **one of the group**. You have no power to direct staff or to decide matters on your own.
**Who it is for:** managers and professionals who are appointed or may be appointed to a board or committee, and officers who support board members.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Understand the board's role and your own
Tell governance from management, and know the documents that give the body its powers.
Meet your duties
Act in good faith, use care, skill and diligence, use powers for their proper purpose and judge independently.
Manage conflicts of interest
Declare interests early, step back from the decision, and keep a register.
Handle gifts, information and the media
Decline improper offers, protect confidential information, and speak for the body only through the agreed spokesperson.
Prepare for and contribute at meetings
Read the papers, ask good questions, support decisions made collectively, and record dissent properly.
Work with the chair, management and the Minister
Challenge and support the CEO, act through the board, and resist private pressure.
Raise concerns
Report suspected wrongdoing to the right person through the right channel.
Manage your time and develop
Plan your commitment, protect your wellbeing, assess your own performance and plan your development.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper**, including short sums on attendance and time.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers.
**Practical tasks**: a group induction guide with personal development plans, and a role play in which each member handles a conduct or conflict scenario with the right written record.

blocks.note: Many questions give you a situation and ask what you should **do**. The best answer is nearly always honest, open, through the proper channel, and in the interest of the body, not yours.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The board, management and your place on the board

ul: Sets **direction**: approves the strategy, plans and budget.
Makes **major decisions** and approves key policies.
Appoints, supports and **appraises the CEO**.
Oversees **performance, risk, controls and finance**.
Ensures **compliance** with the law and government guidance.
**Accounts** for the body to the Minister, Parliament and the public.

head: Aspect
The board (governance)
Management (the CEO and staff)
rows: Question
Are we doing the right things?
Are we doing things right?
Role
Direction, oversight, accountability
Day-to-day running and delivery
Acts through
Collective decisions at meetings
Staff and delegated authority
Example
Approves the budget and the staffing policy
Decides who fills a clerk's post and how files are kept

blocks.p: A board member who visits an office and tells a clerk to change how she files applications has **stepped outside her role**. A single member has **no authority** to direct staff. Concerns about how work is done are raised with the CEO through the chair, or at the board.

blocks.note: The board acts only **together, at a properly called meeting** (or by an approved written resolution). A member is not the board.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: To whom the board is accountable

blocks.p: The board of a public body is accountable, **through the Minister and Parliament, to the public** for how it uses public money and powers. The CEO is accountable to the board, and the board holds the CEO to account.

head: Document
Why you need it
rows: The law that set up the body
Its purpose, powers and limits, and how members are appointed
The body's rules and standing orders
How meetings, voting and committees work
The corporate plan and budget
What the body has promised to deliver and with what money
The latest annual report and audited statements
How the body has performed and its financial position
The code of conduct and conflict-of-interest policy
The standards expected of you
The risk register and recent audit reports
The main threats and what the auditors have found

blocks.p: A **formal induction** teaches a new member the body's purpose, finances, risks, duties, staff, stakeholders and how the board works. It is a short, planned programme, not a quick chat before the first meeting. Read the governing documents **before** your first meeting, meet the chair and CEO, tour the offices and ask for the previous year's papers.

sections.title: Your duties as a board member

blocks.p: Duties come from the law that governs public bodies, the body's own law and rules, and the general standards expected of those who govern. This unit refers to them by purpose and does not quote section numbers. Your instructor will give you the law's exact wording where you need it.

head: Duty
What it means
Example in practice
rows: Good faith and loyalty (fiduciary duty)
Act honestly in the best interests of the **body**, ahead of your own, your business's, your party's or whoever appointed you
You vote for the supplier that gives best value, not the one a friend owns
Care, skill and diligence
Prepare, attend, ask questions and use reasonable judgement, to the level of your knowledge and experience
You read the 40-page paper before the meeting and ask about the costs
Proper purpose and within powers
Use powers only for the purpose they were given, and within the law
You do not use the body's funds for a purpose the law does not allow
Independent judgement
Form your own view on the evidence, free of undue pressure
You do not simply follow the chair, the CEO or the Minister
Confidentiality
Do not share board information that is not public, or use it for personal gain
You do not tell friends about a decision before staff are told
Avoid conflicts
Declare and manage interests
You declare that your cousin owns the building
Collective responsibility
Support the board's decisions once made
You explain the decision as the board's, not as 'theirs'

blocks.p: Putting the body's interests first means putting them ahead of **personal, business or political interests**. If you were appointed by a Minister or a group, you still owe your duty to the **body**, not to them.

You are not expected to be an expert in everything, but you are expected to do what a reasonable person with your experience would do: **prepare, attend, ask, question and think**. If the financial statements are hard for you to understand, ask the finance officer or chair for a briefing and build your skills. Do not nod through what you do not understand.

Board decisions belong to the whole board. Before the decision, you should state your concerns clearly with evidence, and if they are not resolved, ask for your disagreement to be **recorded in the minutes**. After the decision, you **support it publicly as the board's decision**, even if you voted against. If you truly cannot, the honest course is to **resign**. You do not attack the decision in the media or undermine it among staff.

The board may rely on advice from lawyers, accountants, auditors and managers. But **you keep responsibility**. You should understand the advice, test it with questions, and rely on it only after weighing it. 'The lawyer told us' is not a full defence.

Many board members have political views or links. Your board work must be **free of party interest**: you do not make decisions to help or harm a party, and you do not use the body's resources for political ends. When the Minister or a politician asks you privately for a favour, for example to block an appointment or give a contract to a named firm, you **explain that you act through the board**, decline, and tell the chair about the approach.

Boards of public bodies commonly arrange **directors' and officers' liability insurance**. It protects members who act **honestly and with care** against certain legal costs and claims. It does not protect dishonest conduct. It is not an excuse to take less care.

blocks.note: Public bodies in Jamaica work under a law on the management and accountability of public bodies and government's corporate governance guidance. The law sets standards of care and accountability for those who govern. Learn it by purpose.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Conflicts of interest, gifts and information

blocks.h: What is a conflict of interest?

blocks.p: A **conflict of interest** exists when your private interests, or those of someone close to you, could affect, or could appear to affect, your judgement on a board matter.

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: Financial (pecuniary)
You or a close person could gain or lose money
Your husband's firm bids for a contract; a company you own supplies the body
Non-financial
Friendship, family, loyalty or obligation that could sway you
A close friend applies for the CEO post
Perceived (apparent)
A fair-minded observer might think your judgement is affected, even if it is not
You sit on a panel choosing a firm in which a former business partner holds shares
Duty-to-duty
Your duties to two bodies pull in different directions
You serve on two boards that are competing for the same grant

flow: Notice the conflict as soon as you see the agenda or the bid list
Declare it, as early as you can, to the chair or secretary in writing
Follow the body's rules on what is allowed (some interests allow you to stay without voting; most require you to leave)
Leave the room for the discussion and the vote where the rules say so
Check that the minutes record the declaration and your leaving and returning
Keep the register of interests up to date

ul: A **register of interests**, updated each year and when things change, makes interests known in advance so conflicts are spotted early.
A member who is a partner in a law firm should **declare** the interest and take **no part** in the choice of outside lawyers; the firm may compete under the rules like any other.
If you are not sure whether something is a conflict, **declare it**. Disclosure rarely harms you; hiding it can.

blocks.p: A gift or hospitality from someone who deals with the body, or who hopes to win a contract or a decision, may create a sense of obligation or look like a reward or a bribe. **Decline** anything of more than small value, and **report the offer** under the code of conduct (many bodies keep a **gifts and hospitality register**). Small items such as a calendar or a pen offered to everyone may be allowed under the policy; follow it. Do not accept anything while a bid or decision is pending.

Information you learn as a board member belongs to the body. **Using confidential information for personal gain** is a serious breach. For example, learning that the body will buy land in a certain area and buying a plot nearby first is misuse of board information, and may break the law.

ul: Board papers and discussion are **confidential until announced** or released by the board.
Do not discuss matters such as job cuts, appointments or contracts with friends, family or staff before the board releases them.
Keep papers secure: do not leave them at a café table or in a car, or on an unlocked phone or shared computer. Use the board portal if one exists.
Return or destroy papers as the secretary advises when you leave the board.

blocks.p: When a journalist phones you, refer them to the **chair or the agreed spokesperson**. Your personal opinion, even if sensible, can be taken as the body's view or can reveal confidential information. Do not post about board discussions on **social media**; follow the body's communication policy. Remember that 'private' messages can be shared.

sections.title: Preparing for and contributing at meetings

flow: Read the agenda and note which items need decisions
Read the papers in full, not only the summaries
For each decision ask: what is proposed, is the information enough, what are the options, costs and risks, does it fit the plan?
Write your questions and send the difficult ones to the chair or secretary beforehand
Seek missing facts or a briefing if you need it

blocks.p: **Example.** A 40-page paper proposes a J$300,000,000 contract. A responsible member reads it carefully, notes questions, and asks for missing facts before the meeting. A member who only reads the summary has not met the duty of care.

ul: Arrive on time; switch off distractions.
Declare interests when the chair calls for them.
Speak to the point, once, and listen to others.
If you doubt the figures in a proposal and the rest of the board seems in favour, **raise your concern clearly** and ask for it to be recorded if it is not resolved.
Respect colleagues: **courtesy and respect** are part of the code. Never mock a colleague's question.
Vote according to your own judgement.

blocks.p: Committees such as audit, finance and human resources do detailed work for the board. A member with an accounting background asked to join the **audit committee** should understand that she helps the board oversee **financial reporting, controls and audit**, but the decisions remain the board's, unless the rules delegate them.

A board member watches the body's **risks**. If the risk register has not been updated for a year, although a hurricane damaged two offices, she should **raise it at the board** and ask management to review the risks and report back.

Attendance rate = **meetings attended ÷ meetings held × 100**. A member who attended 11 of 15 meetings has attended 11 ÷ 15 = 73.3%. Rules may set a minimum, for example 80% of 15 is **12** meetings. If your work or health means you will miss most meetings for a long period, **discuss it with the chair** and consider stepping down: absence leaves the board short of its quorum and skills.

A board member's hours are **meeting time + reading time + committee time + extras**. Suppose a board meets **8 times** a year for 3 hours, with 5 hours of reading per meeting. The finance committee meets **6 times** for 2 hours, with 3 hours of reading for each meeting. There is a one-day (8-hour) annual planning retreat.

head: Item
Working
Hours
rows: Board meetings and reading
Finance committee
Retreat
**Total**

blocks.p: Add up your own commitment honestly **before** accepting an appointment, then add travel and the demands of your job. Before accepting another board seat, think first about **whether you have the time** and whether the new body creates a conflict with the others.

sections.title: Working with others and raising concerns

blocks.p: The **chair** leads the board and ensures it works well. The **CEO** leads management. The best relationship between board members and the CEO is **constructive challenge and support, with clear roles**: ask hard questions, but do not run the organisation. Take problems with staff to the CEO through the chair.

A member of staff may come to you with a grievance about a manager. You should **listen politely, not promise a result, and refer the person to the proper channel** (the CEO, human resources, the grievance procedure) and tell the chair that an approach has been made. Do not investigate or decide alone: it is management's responsibility and it would put you in the middle of a dispute.

The Minister responsible for the body may give policy direction through the proper channels, and the board must pay attention to it. But a **private request** to block an appointment, or to favour one firm, is not a lawful direction. You explain that you act through the board, decline, and report it to the chair.

If you suspect fraud, misuse of funds or a serious breach, **raise it promptly with the chair or the chair of the audit committee, following the body's procedures**, and give the facts you have, not accusations. Do **not** investigate on your own, question staff, confront the person involved or tell others. Doing so may alert the person, destroy evidence, or be unfair if the claim is false. Keep a written note of what you saw and when. Anonymous complaints should be treated seriously but not assumed true; the board decides how they are checked.

blocks.note: Jamaica has law that protects people who make protected disclosures in good faith about wrongdoing. Follow the body's own procedure for reporting concerns.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **code of conduct** sets out the standards expected of members (honesty, respect, integrity, confidentiality, openness) and how breaches are handled. Read it, sign it and follow it. A breach, for example mocking a colleague, using confidential information, or failing to declare an interest, can lead to a warning or a request to resign, and, in serious cases, the appointing authority may remove a member.

ul: Respect fellow members, staff and the public.
Disagree with ideas, not people.
Treat staff fairly; do not use your position to get favours.
Keep your language and your messages professional, on and off social media.

sections.title: Managing yourself: wellbeing, development and review

blocks.p: Taking on too many roles reduces the quality of each. A member serving on four boards who is exhausted and behind with papers should **review commitments and reduce them to a level he can manage well**, rather than carry on and underperform or miss papers. Plan your year, block time for reading, and be honest with the chair when you are overloaded.
Assessing your own performance each year shows your **strengths and gaps** and lets you plan your development. Use clear questions based on your duties:

ul: Did I **prepare** well for each meeting?
Did I **attend** as expected?
Did I **add value** in the debate, with evidence and sound questions?
Did I **act within my duties**: declare interests, keep confidences, support collective decisions?
Did I **listen** and respect others?
Did I keep my knowledge up to date?

blocks.p: Rate yourself honestly, seek feedback from the chair or a trusted colleague, and note evidence for each rating.

head: Gap
Action
By when
How I will know
rows: Weak on reading financial statements
Take a short course in public-sector accounts; ask the finance officer for a briefing before each quarterly meeting
End of the second quarter
I can explain the budget variances at the next meeting
Rarely speak on strategy items
Prepare one question for each strategy item
Starting next meeting
I ask at least one question at each meeting
Limited governance knowledge
Read national guidance on boards; shadow an experienced member
By the third meeting
I can explain the body's risk register in my own words

blocks.p: A good plan is **specific, dated and checkable**. Suitable development includes a governance course, reading guidance and learning from experienced members.

The chair may ask each member to complete a **board evaluation** survey about how the whole board is performing. Give **honest, specific and constructive** feedback: cite examples, say what would help, and avoid personal attacks. The board reviews the results together and agrees improvements.

When you decide to leave, **resign in writing as the rules require**, return all board papers and equipment, and keep what you learned confidential. If your term ends, hand over any work in progress and pass your knowledge to your successor.

blocks.note: Self-assessment, evaluation and a development plan are not paperwork. They show that you take your duties seriously and that you act on what you learn.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain what a board does and how governance differs from management.
say why a single member has no authority to direct staff.
name the documents a new member should read and what induction should cover.
explain the duties of good faith, care, skill and diligence, proper purpose, independence and confidentiality.
explain collective responsibility, and what a member may do before and after a decision she disagrees with.
explain why I remain responsible when I rely on advice.
identify financial, non-financial and perceived conflicts, and declare and manage them.
handle gifts, hospitality, confidential information, journalists and social media.
prepare for a meeting, contribute well and have my concerns recorded.
work out an attendance rate and my yearly time commitment.
respond properly to a private request from a Minister or a complaint from a staff member.
raise a concern about suspected wrongdoing through the right channel.
complete a self-assessment and write a development plan with dates.
give constructive feedback in a board evaluation.
resign properly and protect confidentiality after I leave.

terms: Board
The group appointed to govern an organisation and to hold management to account.
Governance
Direction, oversight and accountability, carried out by the board.
Fiduciary duty
The duty of trust to act honestly and in the body's best interests.
Duty of care, skill and diligence
The duty to prepare, attend, ask questions and use reasonable judgement.
Collective responsibility
The principle that all members stand behind a board decision once it is made.
Independent member
A member with no material business or family link with the body or its management.
Conflict of interest
A situation where private interests could affect, or appear to affect, official judgement.
Pecuniary interest
A financial interest in a matter.
Perceived conflict
A situation where a fair-minded observer might think judgement could be affected.
Register of interests
The record, kept by the secretary, of members' interests.
Recuse
To withdraw from a discussion or decision because of a conflict of interest.
Code of conduct
A document setting standards of behaviour and how breaches are handled.
Induction
A planned introduction for a new member to the body and the board.
Directors' and officers' liability insurance
Cover for members acting honestly against certain claims about their decisions.
Board evaluation
The yearly review of how well the board and its members have performed.
Protected disclosure
A report of wrongdoing made in good faith through the proper channel, which the law protects.

c1.title: Marcia Henry joins a college council
c1.text: Mrs Marcia Henry, a retired school principal, has been appointed to the council of a state-owned vocational college. The council meets 8 times a year for 3 hours, with about 5 hours of reading for each meeting. She has also been asked to join the finance committee, which meets 6 times a year for 2 hours, with 3 hours of reading for each meeting, and to attend a one-day (8-hour) annual retreat. She has not yet been told anything about her duties.

c2.title: A supplier on the board
c2.text: Mr Trevor Samuels sits on the board of a parish water-services authority and owns a small hardware business. The authority wants to buy pipe fittings worth J$1,200,000, and his shop has been invited to quote. At Christmas, a contractor that regularly works for the authority sends him a gift voucher worth J$15,000 and invites him to a dinner. The contractor is preparing to bid for next year's pipeline work.

c3.title: A vote on merging two training centres
c3.text: The board of a skills agency votes 7 to 3 to merge two training centres in a rural parish. Dr Alicia Reid voted against and put her concerns about transport for trainees on record. Afterwards, a radio presenter invites her to talk about the decision on a call-in programme, and a community leader urges her to 'fight it'.

c4.title: Invoices just below the limit
c4.text: Ms Paulette Grant, a member of an agency's board and its audit committee, is reading the quarterly payment list. She sees that three invoices of J$990,000 each, from the same supplier and for similar work, were paid in the same month. Management's approval limit for a single purchase without competitive quotes is J$1,000,000. When she asks the CEO informally, he says it is 'just routine'.

c5.title: Lloyd Campbell's year in review
c5.text: Mr Lloyd Campbell, an accountant, joined a parish health board a year ago. The board's code says each member should attend at least 80% of its 15 meetings. He attended 11 and prepared for most of them, but he never spoke on strategy items. In his self-assessment he rates his preparation highly and his contribution to strategy poorly.

c6.title: Rev. Hyacinth Clarke and a staff complaint
c6.text: Rev. Hyacinth Clarke is a board member of a regional authority. A clerk, Mr Winston Brown, stops her after church and tells her that his manager treats him unfairly and gives him the worst shifts. A week later a political party organiser phones her, asking her to support a particular candidate for a job at the authority.

questions.q: Before her first meeting, what should Mrs Henry do to understand the council's powers and purpose?
o: Read the Act setting up the council, its rules, plan and annual report
Wait for the first meeting, where the chair will explain everything she needs
Ask the staff to make decisions for her until she feels confident
Read only the minutes of the last meeting, which will tell her what matters
questions.why: Governing documents tell a member what the body may do and how it works. Reading them, along with a formal induction, is the first step in meeting the duty of care.

questions.q: How many hours a year should Mrs Henry plan for her council and committee work, before travel?
questions.why: Council: 8 × (3 + 5) = 64. Finance committee: 6 × (2 + 3) = 30. Retreat: 8. 64 + 30 + 8 = 102 hours. Travel and her other work come on top.

questions.q: Mrs Henry is also invited to join a second board. What should she consider first?
o: Whether the second board pays larger fees than the council does
Whether her friends already sit on it, so that she will feel welcome
Whether she has the time and has no conflict with the council
Whether she can use the experience to raise her profile in the parish
questions.why: Time and conflicts come first. A member who takes on more than she can manage cannot meet her duty of care to either body.

questions.q: What should Mr Samuels do about the invitation to quote for the pipe fittings?
o: Say nothing, since his shop's price is lower than other suppliers' prices
Declare the interest in writing and take no part in the choice of supplier
Quote through his brother's company so that his name does not appear
Quote, but sit in the meeting and vote to show he has nothing to hide
questions.why: His shop gives him a financial interest. He must declare it and withdraw from the decision, so that the choice is made fairly and is seen to be.

questions.q: How should he respond to the gift voucher and the dinner invitation?
o: Keep the voucher but decline the dinner, so it looks less like a favour
Decline both and report the offers under the code of conduct
Accept both, as it is a seasonal gift and the bid has not yet opened
Accept the voucher and give it to a charity, without telling the board
questions.why: A contractor who works for the authority and is about to bid has an interest in his goodwill. Anything of value should be declined and reported, and no gift should be taken while a bid is pending.

questions.q: Mr Samuels' shop quotes the lowest price for the fittings. Does that remove the conflict?
o: No, a low price does not remove the interest; he must still declare it
Yes, because the authority gains from the lower price and so nobody loses
Yes, as long as his shop's price is checked by the CEO afterwards
No, but he may stay and vote if the other members all agree to it
questions.why: A conflict is about his interest in the outcome, not about whether the price is fair. He still declares it and takes no part, so that the decision is clean and seen to be.

questions.q: After the vote, what is Dr Reid's duty regarding the merger?
o: Oppose it openly in the media, because she voted against it
Stay silent and refuse to take part in any work to carry it out
Encourage staff to ask for the vote to be repeated
Support it as the board's decision, or resign if she cannot
questions.why: Collective responsibility means all members stand behind a decision once it is made. She stated her concerns in the right place; if she cannot support it, the honest course is to resign.

questions.q: The radio presenter wants her view on the merger. What should she normally do?
o: Give her personal opinion, and say clearly that it is only her own
Agree to speak, but only about the parts she supported
Refer the presenter to the chair or the agreed spokesperson
Give the presenter the board papers so that the facts are correct
questions.why: Only the chair or an agreed spokesperson speaks for the body. A personal opinion can be taken as the board's view, and may reveal confidential information.

questions.q: Before the vote, what was the right way for Dr Reid to show that she disagreed?
o: Remain silent in the meeting and tell the community leader afterwards
Walk out before the vote, so that the board lacks a quorum
State her concerns in the meeting and ask for them to be minuted
Ask management to change the plan privately before the meeting
questions.why: The board is the place for disagreement. A recorded dissent shows her reasons and protects her, while still leaving the decision a collective one.

questions.q: What is the best first step for Ms Grant?
o: Call the supplier herself to ask why the invoices were split up
Report the pattern to the chair or audit committee chair, as procedure says
Tell the other board members privately that the CEO has done wrong
Wait until the annual audit, since the CEO called it routine work
questions.why: The pattern may be splitting to avoid competition, but she does not yet know. The right step is to report the facts through the proper channel, not to investigate or accuse alone.

questions.q: Why should she NOT question staff and the supplier herself?
o: It could alert those involved, damage evidence or be unfair to someone innocent
It is the CEO's right alone to speak with the suppliers of the agency
Staff are not allowed to speak to board members under any circumstances
A board member is never allowed to see a list of payments made
questions.why: An unplanned investigation may warn the person, destroy evidence and treat people unfairly. The audit committee or auditors can check properly.

questions.q: Which duty is she carrying out by studying the payment list and acting on what she finds?
o: Collective responsibility, which requires her to avoid disagreeing with management
Political neutrality, which prevents members from challenging officers
Confidentiality, which forbids a member from reading financial records
Care, skill and diligence, together with oversight of finance and controls
questions.why: A member who reads the information, notices a pattern and raises it is using care and diligence and helping the board oversee controls.

questions.q: What was Mr Campbell's attendance rate, and did he meet the board's code?
o: 73.3%, and yes, because he attended most meetings
80%, and yes, because he prepared for them
11%, because he attended only 11 meetings
73.3%, and no: the code needs at least 12 meetings
questions.why: 11 ÷ 15 × 100 = 73.3%. At least 80% of 15 is 12 meetings, so 11 falls short.

questions.q: Which entry would be the best part of his development plan?
o: Try to speak up more often as the year goes on, wherever he can
Leave the strategy items to other members who have more experience
Prepare one question per strategy item and ask it from the next meeting
Attend more meetings, whether or not he has prepared for them
questions.why: A good plan is specific, dated and checkable. A named action starting at a set meeting can be reviewed and shows whether he improved.

questions.q: Because Mr Campbell is an accountant, what does the duty of care expect of him on the finance matters before the board?
o: The same level as a member with no financial training at all
Skill in line with his training, so sharper questions on figures
Nothing more than attending the meeting and voting with the majority
That he takes the decisions on finance for the whole board
questions.why: The duty of care is measured against what a reasonable person with the member's own knowledge and experience would do. His accounting skill raises what is expected of him.

questions.q: Mr Brown complains about his manager. What should Rev. Clarke do?
o: Listen, promise nothing, refer him to the proper channel and tell the chair
Speak to the manager herself and ask for him to be given better shifts
Promise Mr Brown that the board will investigate and put matters right
Ask other staff what they think of the manager before she takes any action
questions.why: A single member has no authority to direct staff. Handling a grievance belongs to management and the procedures; she refers him on and informs the chair.

questions.q: The party organiser asks for her support for a candidate. What principle should guide her?
o: Judge on merit and keep party interests out of board decisions
Support the candidate if the party helped to get her appointed
Support the candidate but keep it secret from the other members
Refuse to take part in any appointment on the board in future
questions.why: A member owes her duty to the body, not to a party. Appointments are made on merit by the board through its procedures.

questions.q: The authority's CEO asks Rev. Clarke to approve a staff reorganisation privately, to save time before the board meets. What should she say?
o: That she will approve it now, as long as she tells the other members afterwards
That she will approve it if the Minister's office agrees to it first
That she will sign a note of approval and the board can confirm it later
That the whole board decides at a meeting; she can discuss it, not approve alone
questions.why: A member is not the board. Decisions are made collectively at a proper meeting, or by an approved written resolution, so one member cannot approve on her own.

questions.q: A member says, 'The lawyer told the board the contract was fine, so I do not need to understand it.' What is wrong with this view?
o: Nothing is wrong, because a board can rely on any expert without questions
Lawyers' advice should never be used by a public-body board
Members stay responsible and should weigh advice before relying on it
Only the chair is responsible for understanding advice for the board
questions.why: A board may rely on professional advice but remains responsible. Each member should understand the advice, ask questions and weigh it before voting.

questions.q: A member of a board sits on three other boards and now falls behind with papers. What is the best response?
o: Skim the papers and rely on the chair's summary of each one
Review his commitments and cut them to what he can manage well
Resign from whichever one of the boards pays the least in fees
Continue as before, as he will catch up when things settle
questions.why: A member must be able to do the job well. If the workload is too heavy, the responsible step is to reduce it rather than let the quality of the work fall.
